title: Where is Hollywood at in 2023, and where is it going in 2024?

commenti.body: I'm not convinced that superhero movies are dead or that anything other than adjacent franchise blockbusters will take their place. Barbie is itself an advertisement for a product, whatever else might be said about it, and the success of Oppenheimer to a large degree can be traced back to the fact that Nolan is one of the biggest names in blockbusters after he blew up with a particularly significant superhero movie. Budgets are about to drop precipitously as a result of AI dramatically reducing CGI workloads.

Hollywood goes where the money is. For a long time the money was at the self aware superhero franchises. This year those made slightly less money. So maybe this is the start of something new? If it is, whatever is coming next probably isn't any better. It will be something even more profitable than cinematic universes with cheap stories and lots of action figures.

Barbenheimer was a great success because both movies had like a trillion dollars in marketing. It got shoved down our throats so hard that it was impossible to avoid.

Anyways, I will keep my attention away from the box office, and more directed towards movies that feel like they are projects of passion. If 2024 doesn't provide enough good movies, there's always the past 100 years of cinema yet to explore.

> I do predict however that blockbuster budgets have peaked and soon will drop as AI threatens to slash VFX costs.

I welcome more mid-budget (and lower) movies, I just hope that VFX artists unionize and are taken more care of.  Not necessarily having their workforce cut down in lieu of using an AI program instead.
The superhero genre will rebound, but it’s going to be a significant reboot. A return to roots of having stakes.
Yeah, but we both know which is more likely.

> If 2024 doesn't provide enough good movies, there's always the past 100 years of cinema yet to explore.

This year, my physical media collection grew, and I rarely went out to the theaters, although I love going.  I tried to make an effort to see major release movies that could use a little help, like Cocaine Bear, Godzilla Minus One, and next week I plan to see the Iron Claw.  Unfortunately I'm not currently near any arthouse theaters, so all I can do is theatrically support comedies, dramas, and foreign movies with what I have access to.
It's over, brother. The ship has sailed and it's not coming back. The people have had enough.

For me personally 2024 will be the year that Hollywood and I part ways. I've made the New Years' resolution to watch no US-corporate entertainment over the next year, at least. 

American indie films will be immune from this taboo but anything that comes from the major studios or is commissioned by streaming services will be struck off the nightly menu. 

I'm hoping to really delve into the delights of world cinema, indie cinema and arthouse cinema and I have no more time for the big-league stuff.

I can honestly say I didn’t think there was a single good film this year. The big serious films like Oppenheimer and Killers of the Flower Moon didn’t do it for me. Old favorites like Wes Anderson bored me. Fun thrash like Barbie also bored me. I avoid superhero movies like the plague. I am beginning to feel that the medium is played out, and nothing is new and novel any more.

* Teetering on the brink of collapse. Hollywood simply can't keep up with changing technology.

* The whole industry has been reeling from 'one disaster to the next' since the advent of digital. 

* Furthermore, the whole modern-day 'blockbuster' business model is built over a precipice. 

* Ever since 'Raiders', Hollywood has been "building on sand" --just as William Goldman called out at the time.

* Both George Lucas and Stephen Spielberg have caroled warnings; but their cautions have fallen on deaf ears.

* Hollywood is capitalism at it's clumsy worst.

I genuinely believe we’re going to see a lot of great 10-30 million dollar movies make a comeback and an influx of really good indie movies outside the traditional Hollywood system.

The technology is so much cheaper than it’s ever been and the amount of people trying to create is more than it’s ever been. Talk to Me was a $4.5m budget, it was written and directed by 2 guys who did Aussie TV narrative work and a YouTube channel. The Creator was shot on a $4000 camera, the Fx3 with vintage lenses and it looked damn good.

There’s an indie movie coming out called I Think I’m Sick and it was written and directed by a Youtuber in Philly. It was produced through Kickstarter and private funding from another YouTuber and they did it all with no real Hollywood experience. And it looks really good, not like an indie short film, it looks like a real theatrical release. I obviously haven’t seen it yet, but I’m very interested in it from the production side of things.

I think we’re going to enter an era of low budget storytelling movies. There will always be massive blockbusters, but for every new Mission Impossible (which I love), there will be 5 Tár’s.

I think the big takeaway from this year is that slapping the logo of a major IP on a movie no longer guarantees commercial success. 

Marvel, DC, Indiana Jones, Mission Impossible—a few years ago, those all would have been major hits, regardless of quality. But between inflation and streaming, people aren’t wasting their time and money anymore to go out and see “ Generic Marvel Movie No. 48”

The biggest hits of the year—Barbie and Oppenheimer—succeeded because of their unique artistic vision, strong critical reviews, and ability to generate popular buzz. They became most-see “event movies” like Marvel was five years ago.

I’m hoping what studios will take away from this is that audiences will now only see *good movies* in theaters, not just big-budget IP that’s been reverse-engineered by a committee of execs. 

Of course, what studios actually *will* take away from this is that they need to make a Polly Pocket movie and an Einstein spin-off.
